claims.text: Adding a small amount of Ti to NbMoTaW or NbMoTaWV will improve the strength–plasticity combination.
The improvement from Ti addition will occur through enhanced grain-boundary cohesion.
NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV have high strength but are brittle at room temperature.
The reference refractory HEA is produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering.
A modest Ti addition should be introduced during alloy synthesis.
The comparison should use identical processing and mechanical-testing conditions at room and elevated temperatures.
Ti addition will improve grain-boundary chemistry and cohesion through segregation or solid-solution effects.
The proposed grain-boundary changes will reduce intergranular brittleness.
Ti will reduce grain-boundary energy and enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion will delay crack initiation and propagation.
The Ti-induced boundary modification will permit dislocation activity and promote a more ductile failure mode.
The Ti addition will not severely compromise the high strength supplied by the refractory elements.
The Ti-modified alloy will gain approximately 10 percentage points of plastic strain, potentially reaching about 11.5% ductility.
The Ti-modified alloy will retain yield strength close to that of the unmodified alloy, with at most a modest decrement.
The beneficial effect will occur only over a limited Ti-concentration range.
Excess Ti may produce unwanted phases or embrittlement.
The optimal Ti concentration and the magnitude of the plasticity improvement are not yet determined.
Processing route and alloy-system differences may change the outcome.
A controlled comparison of the base and Ti-added alloys should measure yield strength, fracture strain, grain-boundary characteristics, and secondary phases.
The hypothesis is falsified if Ti addition gives less than about a 5–10% plastic-strain increase without preserving yield strength, or if detrimental Ti-rich phases appear.
